summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: The bill would let the Chief Executive Medicare cancel certain debts owed by dentists under the old Chronic Disease Dental Scheme.
It would also update the Child Dental Benefits Schedule by adding compliance powers and allowing reviews of suspected poor practice.
The waiver applies to services before 1 April 2010 if all legal requirements were met, and to later services if the dentist shows intent to follow the rules.
changes: Creates a waiver provision for debts under the Medicare Chronic Disease Dental Scheme.
Amends the Dental Benefits Act 2008 to add compliance powers for the Child Dental Benefits Schedule.
Extends the Professional Services Review scheme to dental services under the Child Dental Benefits Schedule.
Allows the Chief Executive Medicare and Department of Human Services staff to get documents from dentists to verify payments.
Makes machinery changes to the Dental Benefits Act, including clarifying protected information disclosure and updating the definition of 'dental provider'.
summary.affected: Dentists who provided services under the Chronic Disease Dental Scheme and children aged 2 to 17 eligible for the Child Dental Benefits Schedule.

speeches.speaker: Peter Dutton
speeches.brief: Introduced the Dental Benefits Legislation Amendment Bill 2014, allowing faster waiver of debts owed by dentists over paperwork errors under the former Chronic Disease Dental Scheme, which provided benefits of up to $4,250 over two years and delivered more than 20 million services to over one million patients before Labor closed it in 2012, and made compliance changes to the $1,000 Child Dental Benefits Schedule.

speeches.speaker: Catherine King
speeches.brief: Argued that Labor's 2012 Dental Reform Package, the biggest investment in dental care since Federation at $4.1 billion, delivered treatment to more than 84,000 children in the Child Dental Benefits Schedule's first two months, including 26,000 outside major cities, and cited findings that people earning over $60,000 a year have seven more teeth on average than those earning under $20,000.

speeches.speaker: Andrew Nikolic
speeches.brief: Argued in support of the Dental Benefits Legislation Amendment Bill 2014, recounting a young Launceston woman in her 20s who fell through a 13-month gap in dental coverage after the Chronic Disease Dental Scheme closed in November 2012, and who needed a local Lions Club to raise $3,000 for her treatment.

speeches.speaker: Shayne Neumann
speeches.brief: Argued that the government's $390 million delay to adult public dental funding and $229 million cut to Labor's dental flexible grants program show its lack of commitment to oral health, and recalled that the Howard government's Chronic Disease Dental Scheme was budgeted at $90 million a year but ended up costing $80 million a month, reaching $248 million by June 2008.

speeches.speaker: Steve Irons
speeches.brief: Defended the Chronic Disease Dental Scheme, contrasting Labor's complaints about its $80 million monthly cost with the $1 billion a month the government now pays in interest on inherited debt, and cited figures showing household health costs rose 35 per cent, gas prices 71 per cent and electricity prices 101 per cent during six years of Labor government.

speeches.speaker: Clare O'Neil
speeches.brief: Defended Labor's $4.1 billion 2012 dental reform package, including $2.7 billion for 3.4 million children and $1.3 billion for 1.4 million low-income adults, and cited figures showing people earning more than $60,000 a year have seven more teeth on average than Australia's poorest, while noting dentists are twice as concentrated in major cities as outer regional areas and triple that of remote areas.

speeches.speaker: Bob Baldwin
speeches.brief: Argued in support of the Dental Benefits Legislation Amendment Bill 2014, which waives paperwork-related debts for dentists under the axed Chronic Disease Dental Scheme, which provided over 17 million services to about one million patients worth up to $4,250 over two years between 2007 and 2012, and cited findings that nearly one in five Australians put off dental care due to cost, rising to one in four in poorer communities.

speeches.speaker: Bob Katter
speeches.brief: Argued that patients in remote North Queensland towns have resorted to pulling their own teeth with pliers after years-long dental waiting lists, despite federal health spending in Queensland rising more than 300 per cent over a decade, and cited the Bundaberg Hospital 'Doctor Death' scandal as evidence of a culture where health workers who speak up are punished.

speeches.speaker: Nick Champion
speeches.brief: Argued that oral health remains the missing link in Medicare, noting the Howard government's Chronic Disease Dental Scheme was meant to cost $90 million a year but ended up costing $80 million a month, and citing figures showing 20,000 children are hospitalised annually for avoidable dental issues and untreated tooth decay affects 37.6 per cent of people in remote areas compared with 23.5 per cent in major cities.

speeches.speaker: Craig Kelly
speeches.brief: Defended the Dental Benefits Legislation Amendment Bill 2014, arguing health spending is rising nine per cent a year, worth an extra $1.3 billion this financial year, and recalling that lowering company tax from 36 to 30 per cent after Labor's inherited $96 billion debt actually increased revenue, funding the Chronic Disease Dental Scheme that delivered 20 million services to over one million Australians.

speeches.speaker: Matt Thistlethwaite
speeches.brief: Supported the Dental Benefits Legislation Amendment Bill 2014, defending Labor's August 2012 six-year, $4 billion dental reform package, which included $2.7 billion for 3.4 million children and $1.3 billion for 1.4 million adult services, and reported that the resulting Child Dental Benefits Schedule treated more than 84,000 children in its first two months, including 26,000 outside major cities.

speeches.speaker: Warren Snowdon
speeches.brief: Explained the Dental Benefits Legislation Amendment Bill would extend Professional Services Review compliance oversight to the Child Dental Benefits Schedule, which caps benefits at $1,000 per child over two years, and cited findings that almost 20,000 children are hospitalised annually for avoidable dental problems and that by age 15 six in ten children have tooth decay.

speeches.speaker: Tanya Plibersek
speeches.brief: Defended Labor's Child Dental Benefits Schedule, which gives about three million children aged two to 17 up to $1,000 in dental benefits over two years and delivered over 1.5 million services in its first five months, described a mother too ashamed of her missing teeth to attend her son's first day of high school, and accused the government of cutting $400 million from public dental schemes in the 2014 budget.

speeches.speaker: Peter Dutton
speeches.brief: Defended the Chronic Disease Dental Scheme introduced in 2007, noting it provided more than 20 million services to over one million patients, 80 per cent of them concession card holders, and criticised the Gillard government for shutting it down and pursuing dentists over minor paperwork errors rather than fixing the scheme's design.
